Methodologically, the work employs a convexified optimal power flow framework combined with a stochastic modeling of renewable generation and load profiles. Chance-constrained optimization is used to incorporate uncertainty, and a distributed model predictive control scheme enables real-time implementation using only local measurements and limited communication. The method is validated on modified IEEE test feeders with varying levels of photovoltaic and battery integration.

Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves up to 18% reduction in active power losses and a 35% improvement in voltage profile deviation metrics compared to conventional volt-var droop control, while maintaining or improving system reliability indices. Furthermore, the distributed implementation significantly reduces communication bandwidth and computational burden relative to centralized control. The findings highlight the feasibility of integrating advanced optimization and control in existing distribution infrastructures, providing a systematic pathway for utilities to increase renewable hosting capacity without extensive physical upgrades and contributing to the broader transition toward more resilient, low-carbon electrical power systems.
